system_message:
You are generating a synthetic but clinically grounded
conversation for exactly one hospital admission.

Rules:
1. Use only facts supported by the provided admission context.
2. The discharge notes are the backbone of the hospital-course
   narrative. Use them first.
3. The ordered problem list should shape the main clinical focus.
4. Radiology, procedures, microbiology, and the previous-admission
   summary are supporting context, not a checklist.
5. Not every packet item needs to appear in the conversation.
6. Speakers must be exactly: Doctor and Patient.
7. Every conversation line must contain:
   - turn number
   - exact timestamp
   - speaker
   - text
8. Timestamps must be monotonically increasing and stay within the
   admission start and admission end times.
9. Keep the conversation medically plausible and understandable to
   a patient.
10. Use short natural exchanges, patient questions, clarifications,
    explanations, reassurance, and follow-up discussion.
11. Do not invent unsupported diagnoses, procedures, test findings,
    or outcomes.
12. Do not mention the dataset, packet, note types, or that the
    conversation is synthetic.
13. Generate the conversation first, then write the summary strictly from the generated conversation_lines.
14. Every claim in summary.summary_paragraph and every item in summary.problems must be explicitly supported by the conversation_lines.
15. Return output that exactly matches the required JSON schema.
task_message:
Generate one rich patient-doctor conversation for this admission and one admission summary.

Generation guidance:
- Approximate stay length: 1 day(s).
- Recommended turn range: 18-28 turns.
- Exact admission window: 2116-01-09 02:43:00 to 2116-01-09 18:49:00.
- Focus first on the discharge-note storyline and the core admission problems.
- Use radiology, procedures, and microbiology only as supporting detail when they help the story.
- Do not try to mention every packet item.
- Let the conversation unfold across admission, mid-course updates, and discharge planning.
- Prefer many short natural exchanges over a few long summary turns.
- The patient should ask questions, express concerns, seek clarification, and respond to updates throughout the stay.
- The doctor should explain results, treatment changes, progress, and follow-up in multiple conversational beats over time.
- You may paraphrase and add natural conversational glue, but do not invent unsupported diagnoses, procedures, findings, or outcomes.
- Generate the conversation first, then derive the final summary only from the conversation_lines you wrote.
- The final summary must contain admission start time, admission end time, one paragraph summary, and a list of problems.
- Final self-check before returning JSON: turn_number contiguous from 1; conversation_lines.time nondecreasing and inside the exact admission window; summary.admission_start and summary.admission_end copied exactly from the packet; no conversation line has empty text.

previous_admission_summary_used.summary_paragraph: Mr. Johnson, a man with a history of systolic heart failure (EF 15%), atrial fibrillation, hypertension, and alcohol abuse, was admitted with chest pain and dizziness after reporting multiple episodes of AICD firing, which was later ruled out. He had a significant drop in hematocrit from baseline to 26.6%, prompting concern for internal bleeding due to a recent altercation involving abdominal and head trauma. CT scans of the head and abdomen showed no acute hemorrhage. He was transfused one unit of packed red blood cells for symptomatic anemia, with improvement in hemoglobin to 10.8 g/dL by discharge. Chest pain was determined to be musculoskeletal, not cardiac or infectious, and resolved with acetaminophen. Pradaxa was held initially but restarted at discharge due to high thrombotic risk. Alcohol withdrawal was managed supportively, and the patient declined referral to a treatment program. He was discharged home in stable condition with clear instructions to avoid alcohol and seek immediate care after any fall or trauma.

Please do NOT take Pradaxa or Aspirin while you are taking

radiology_notes.text:
INDICATION:  ___ male with chest pain.

COMPARISON:  Chest radiograph from ___ and CT chest from ___.

CHEST, AP:  Right ventricular pacemaker/defibrillator courses in expected
position.  Lung volumes remain low, with crowding of bronchovascular markings.
There is increased elevation of the right hemidiaphragm, with adjacent right
lower lobe opacity.  New central venous congestion and increased small
bilateral effusions, right greater than left.  Moderate-to-severe cardiomegaly
persists.  

IMPRESSION:
1.  Congestive heart failure.
2.  Moderate-to-severe cardiomegaly.
3.  Right lower lobe atelectasis, which can be seen with acute pulmonary
embolism.  Please refer to subsequent CT for further details.

INDICATION:  Evaluation of patient with chest pain, hemoptysis, and
tachycardia.

COMPARISON:  CT torso from ___.

TECHNIQUE:  MDCT-acquired axial images were obtained from the thoracic inlet
to the base of the lungs prior to administration of IV contrast.  Following
the administration of 100 mL of Omnipaque nonionic intravenous contrast,
MDCT-acquired axial images were obtained from the thoracic inlet to the base
of the lungs.  1.25- and 5-mm collimated images were prepared and reviewed. 
Multiplanar reformatted images were also prepared and reviewed.

FINDINGS:

CHEST CTA:

Opacification of the pulmonary vasculature demonstrates focal filling defects
in the posterior basal segment pulmonary arteries of the right lower lobe
suggestive of a pulmonary embolus in this region (3:44, 46, 603b:39). 
Otherwise, the remainder of the pulmonary vasculature is without any focal
filling defect to suggest a pulmonary embolus.  

Adjacent to the filling defect in the right posterior basal segment, there is
a focal opacity with a mixture of ground galss and confluent opacities (3:54)
which corresponds anatomically to the area of the pulmonary embolus and
consistent with a pulmonary infarct. 

Otherwise, the remainder of the lungs is clear without any focal opacities. 
Previously visualized small-to-moderate right pleural effusion remains stable.
Previously visualized small left pleural effusion has now resolved.

There is no evidence of right heart strain.  The interventricular septum
remains deviated convexly towards the right ventricle.  The pulmonary artery
does not appear dilated.  Single-lead pacemaker appears in place. Heart
remains stably enlarged. 

The previously visualized right pleural effusion has increased in size. The
previously visualized left pleural effusion has resolved. 

A few prominent mediastinal lymph nodes are visualized and likely reactive.
But there is no hilar, mediastinal, or axillary lymphadenopathy by CT size
criteria.

There are no suspicious lytic or sclerotic osseous lesions.

This study is not tailored for evaluation of subdiaphragmatic structures;
however, the visualized portions of the upper liver, spleen, and kidneys
appear normal.

IMPRESSION:
1.  There is evidence of an acute pulmonary embolism in the posterior basal
segment of the right lower lobe.  Additionally, adjacent opacity in the same
anatomical segment correponds to the pulmonary infarct.  However, there is no
evidence of right heart strain or other pulmonary emboli.
2.  Mild increase in small to moderate right pleural effusion may be due to
the pulmonary embolism.
3.  Stable moderate cardiomegaly.
4.  Resolution of previously seen small left pleural effusion.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Mr. Johnson, I'm Dr. Patel. You're in the hospital now because you came in with chest pain and coughing up blood. Do you remember coming to the ER earlier?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Yeah… I was at Stop and Shop with my sister and started coughing blood. I didn’t want to stay at first, but then I felt dizzy and threw up blood. Is it serious?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: It is serious. We did a CT scan of your chest, and it showed a blood clot in your lung—what we call a pulmonary embolism. That’s likely why you’re coughing up blood and having chest pain.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: A clot? But I’m on Pradaxa for my heart rhythm. Shouldn’t that prevent clots?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You're right, Pradaxa helps, but sometimes clots still happen. Since this is a pulmonary embolism, we need to switch you to a different blood thinner—Coumadin—for a while, with injections called Lovenox to start.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: So I can’t stay on my usual meds? What about my water pill and blood pressure meds?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’re keeping you on your blood pressure and heart medications—metoprolol, losartan, and furosemide. But we held the furosemide tonight because your blood pressure was a bit low.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Okay… but I don’t feel that bad now. Can I just go home and take the pills there?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: I understand, but this is dangerous. A clot in the lung can be life-threatening. We want to monitor you and start treatment properly here.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I just… I don’t like being in the hospital. I haven’t had a drink in 15 days. I’m not drunk or anything.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Your tox screen didn’t show alcohol, but we did see benzodiazepines. You said you haven’t taken any—can you confirm that?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: No, I didn’t take any. Maybe someone gave me a pill, but I don’t know. I just feel tired and confused.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We think it might be related to your history of alcohol use and possible withdrawal. We’ve started you on thiamine and folic acid, and we’re watching you closely.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Mr. Johnson, the CT confirmed a clot in the lower part of your right lung. There’s also some fluid around it, which is common with this kind of clot. The good news is your heart isn’t strained, and the clot isn’t massive.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: So it’s not that bad? Maybe I really can go home.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: It’s still dangerous. If the clot gets worse or another forms, it could be fatal. We strongly recommend you stay. But if you choose to leave, you must understand the risks.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I understand. I could die. But I want to go home. I’ll do the shots and take the Coumadin.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Alright. We’ll discharge you against medical advice. You’ll get Lovenox injections twice a day and Coumadin once daily. Do not take Pradaxa or aspirin with it—they can interact.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Got it. No Pradaxa, no aspirin. Just Coumadin and the shots.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Exactly. And you need to get your INR checked on ___ at ___—that’s a blood test to make sure the Coumadin is working right.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’ll go. I don’t want to end up back here.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Also, keep taking your other meds—metoprolol, furosemide, losartan, simvastatin, and your Prilosec. And please avoid alcohol completely.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I know, I know. I’ve been trying. No more drinking.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: One more thing—weigh yourself every morning. If you gain more than three pounds in a day, call your doctor. That could mean your heart is struggling.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Okay, I’ll do that. Thanks, doc. I get it’s serious. I’ll follow the plan.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Good. We’re giving you all the supplies and prescriptions. If you have chest pain, shortness of breath, or cough up more blood, go to the ER immediately.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I will. I don’t want to go through this again.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’re alert and making an informed choice. We respect that. Please take care of yourself, Mr. Johnson.

summary.summary_paragraph: Mr. Johnson, a man with a history of systolic heart failure, atrial fibrillation, hypertension, and alcohol abuse, was admitted with chest pain and hemoptysis. A CT scan revealed an acute pulmonary embolism in the right lower lobe with associated pulmonary infarct and pleural effusion. He was started on anticoagulation with Lovenox and prescribed Coumadin for long-term management, with Pradaxa and aspirin discontinued. Despite clear explanation of the life-threatening risks, he chose to leave against medical advice. At discharge, he was alert, oriented, and demonstrated understanding of his treatment plan, including medication instructions and the need for INR monitoring. He was sent home with prescriptions and strict instructions to avoid alcohol and seek immediate care for worsening symptoms.
